analysis.one_liner: Bars most lawsuits over accidents from workplace and business equipment more than 18 years after it was first sold.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 222-194 on February 2, 2000, but the Senate never voted on it, so it died and never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a federal 18-year cutoff for lawsuits over durable goods used in a trade or business — machinery, equipment, and similar products. After 18 years from a product's first sale, a person hurt or killed in an accident involving it could no longer sue the maker or seller, as long as they could get workers' compensation and the injury was not from a toxic substance like asbestos. Suits for property damage would be barred outright after 18 years, and the federal cutoff would override more generous state laws. The House passed it on a near-party-line vote, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted, so it died at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of workplace and business equipment — industrial machinery, farm and construction equipment, and similar durable goods — gain because they stop facing lawsuits over products more than 18 years old, no matter when the accident happened. Their liability insurers gain because long-tail claims they might have to pay disappear. Companies that kept a product in the field for decades would no longer answer for harm it caused years later.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Makers of industrial and business equipment

how_it_helps.text: Sets an absolute 18-year limit, counted from the product's first sale, for lawsuits over property damage from accidents involving durable business goods [S5].
Bars injury and death suits after 18 years when the injured person has received or is eligible for workers' compensation and the harm is not toxic harm such as asbestos [S3].
Overrides any state statute of repose, imposing the 18-year federal cutoff nationwide even in states that allow longer periods to sue [S5].
Exempts passenger-carrying vehicles (cars, buses, planes, trains for hire), honors written express warranties longer than 18 years, and leaves environmental cleanup claims unaffected [S5].

analysis.who_pays: People injured, or families of people killed, in accidents involving workplace or business equipment more than 18 years after its first sale, who would be limited to workers' compensation benefits instead of a court judgment. Workers' compensation typically pays medical bills and part of lost wages but not damages for pain, suffering, or full lost income. Owners whose property is destroyed by old equipment would lose their claim entirely.

drawbacks.text: A worker injured by an 19-year-old machine could only collect workers' compensation — medical care and a share of lost wages — and could not recover in court for pain, suffering, or losses that exceed those benefits [S5].

Property damage claims are barred entirely after 18 years with no workers' compensation substitute, leaving an owner whose business is destroyed by old equipment with no recourse against a defective maker [S5].
The bill is retroactive in effect: it takes away claims for accidents that already happened, giving claimants only a one-year window after enactment to file under prior law [S5].

A good-faith supporter would argue this is a fair trade: manufacturers cannot warranty equipment forever, witnesses and records fade over decades, and workers' compensation remains the designed safety net for workplace injuries. But the bill covers equipment used by businesses beyond just their own workers — for example, an injured bystander or a contractor's employee would also be cut off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to manufacturers and insurers, who would shed liability for the oldest equipment they sold — the claims most likely to involve aging, poorly maintained, or defective machines. The costs fall on the small number of people seriously hurt by old equipment, who lose access to full court compensation. Because claims after 18 years are rare but often severe, and because workers' compensation replaces only part of what a lawsuit can recover, the bill shifts real costs from companies onto injured people. The carve-outs for asbestos and environmental claims prevent some of the worst exposures, but the core trade favors sellers of equipment over the people it injures.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 222-194 in February 2000, but the Senate referred it to its Commerce Committee, which never brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Steve Chabot in June 1999 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1].
The Judiciary Committee approved it on a narrow 16-14 vote and reported it in amended form in October 1999 [S3].
The House passed the bill on February 2, 2000, by a vote of 222-194, with Republicans voting 198-17 in favor and Democrats voting 23-176 against [S8].
The Senate received the bill on February 3, 2000, and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured workers and their families came out better off because the bill died: they kept the right to sue manufacturers of old equipment in every state. Manufacturers and their insurers did not get the 18-year liability shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured workers kept their right to sue

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split sharply by party: 198 of 221 Republicans voted yes and 176 of 211 Democrats voted no, with only 23 Democrats in favor.

industries.note: The bill would let makers of machinery and equipment stop answering in court for accidents involving products sold more than 18 years earlier, shifting those costs onto injured people who would be limited to workers' compensation. Asbestos claims and environmental cleanup claims are carved out, so the shield would not extend to toxic-harm litigation.

A hard 18-year cutoff removes the long-tail claims insurers price into premiums, letting them collect premiums for decades-old products without ever paying the rare late-injury claims. The cost reduction comes at the expense of injured claimants, not through any added public benefit.

The bar on late claims would eliminate a category of injury cases these lawyers bring on behalf of hurt workers and their families. Their interest runs alongside the people they represent, who would lose court access.
